learn.hook: Drop a pebble in a pond: the ripple's radius grows at a steady 5 cm/s, but its area grows faster and faster. Derivatives tell you exactly how fast.
points: Derivatives help us study rates of change, where functions rise or fall, and their highest and lowest values.
dy/dx is the rate of change of y with respect to x; its value at x = x₀ is the rate at that instant.
If x and y both depend on t, then dy/dt = (dy/dx)(dx/dt), and dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt).
Circle: A = πr², dA/dr = 2πr. Sphere: V = (4/3)πr³, dV/dr = 4πr²; S = 4πr², dS/dr = 8πr.
Cube of edge x: V = x³, dV/dt = 3x² dx/dt; S = 6x², dS/dt = 12x dx/dt. Cone: V = (1/3)πr²h.

example.q: The volume of a cube increases at 9 cm³/s. How fast is its surface area increasing when an edge is 10 cm?
steps: V = x³ ⇒ dV/dt = 3x² dx/dt ⇒ 9 = 3(100) dx/dt ⇒ dx/dt = 3/100 cm/s.

learn.reallife: During the monsoon, dam engineers estimate how fast a reservoir's water level is rising from the rate of inflow, a classic related-rates calculation.

games.title: Quantity ↔ rate formula
pairs: Surface area of sphere w.r.t. r
Volume of cube w.r.t. edge x
Surface area of cube w.r.t. edge x

games.title: Rate truths
items: If dA/dt is negative, A is decreasing at that instant.
A negative rate means the quantity is falling.
For a circle, dA/dr = πr.
dA/dr = 2πr.
dy/dt = (dy/dx)(dx/dt) when y depends on x and x on t.
This is the chain rule.
If the radius of a circle grows at a constant rate, its area also grows at a constant rate.
dA/dt = 2πr dr/dt grows with r.
The rate of change of volume of a sphere with respect to r equals its surface area.
dV/dr = 4πr² = surface area.

quiz.q: Find the rate of change of the area of a circle with respect to its radius when r = 5 cm.
quiz.explain: dA/dr = 2πr = 2π(5) = 10π.
quiz.mistake: Uses A = πr² itself instead of its derivative

quiz.q: The radius of a circle increases at 3 cm/s. At what rate (in cm²/s) is the area increasing when r = 10 cm?
quiz.explain: dA/dt = 2πr dr/dt = 2π(10)(3) = 60π cm²/s.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the factor 2 from d(r²)/dr

quiz.q: A stone dropped in a pond makes ripples whose radius grows at 5 cm/s. How fast is the enclosed area growing when r = 8 cm?
quiz.explain: dA/dt = 2πr dr/dt = 2π(8)(5) = 80π cm²/s.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies r by the rate without the factor 2π

quiz.q: Find dV/dr for a sphere when r = 10 cm.
quiz.explain: V = (4/3)πr³ ⇒ dV/dr = 4πr² = 400π.
quiz.mistake: Gives the volume instead of its rate

quiz.q: The edge of a cube increases at 3 cm/s. How fast (in cm³/s) is its volume increasing when the edge is 10 cm?
quiz.explain: dV/dt = 3x² dx/dt = 3(100)(3) = 900 cm³/s.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to multiply by dx/dt or by 3

quiz.q: The total area of a square changes at 8 cm²/s when its side is 4 cm. At what rate (cm/s) is the side changing?
quiz.explain: A = s² ⇒ dA/dt = 2s ds/dt ⇒ 8 = 8 ds/dt ⇒ ds/dt = 1 cm/s.
quiz.mistake: Divides by s instead of 2s

quiz.q: If y = x² + 2x and x increases at 3 units/s, how fast (in units/s) does y increase when x = 2?
quiz.explain: dy/dt = (2x + 2) dx/dt = (6)(3) = 18 units/s.
quiz.mistake: Uses dy/dx = 6 and forgets to multiply by dx/dt

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): When a spherical balloon's radius increases at a constant rate, its volume increases faster as it grows.
Reason (R): dV/dt = 4πr² dr/dt, which increases with r.
options: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.explain: With dr/dt fixed, dV/dt is proportional to r², so it increases with r. R gives exactly that reason.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a constant radius rate means a constant volume rate

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'If the radius of a circle grows steadily, how do I find how fast the area grows?'
teach.praise: Tweet! dA/dt = 2πr × dr/dt. The bigger the circle, the faster the area grows!
teach.nudge: What do you multiply dA/dr by to get the rate with respect to time?

topics.title: Related rates in action; marginal cost and revenue

learn.hook: A ladder slides down a wall; sand piles into a cone; a factory adds one more unit. Each is one equation, differentiated with respect to time or quantity.
points: Strategy: draw a diagram, name variables, write an equation linking them, differentiate with respect to t, then substitute the given values.
Ladder of length L: x² + y² = L² ⇒ x dx/dt + y dy/dt = 0.
Use a fixed ratio (like h = r/6 in a sand cone) to reduce to one variable before differentiating.
Marginal cost MC = dC/dx: approximate cost of producing one more unit. Marginal revenue MR = dR/dx.
A negative rate means the quantity is decreasing, e.g. the top of the ladder moving down.

example.q: A 5 m ladder leans against a wall. Its foot is pulled away at 2 cm/s. How fast does the top slide down when the foot is 4 m from the wall?
steps: 4(2) + 3 dy/dt = 0 ⇒ dy/dt = −8/3 cm/s (units of the rate stay cm/s).
example.answer: The top slides down at 8/3 cm/s.

learn.reallife: An Indian textile mill uses marginal cost to decide whether producing one more batch of cotton fabric will add more to cost than to revenue.

games.title: Solve a related-rates problem
items: Draw a diagram and name the variables
Write an equation linking the variables
Differentiate both sides with respect to t
Substitute the known values and rates
Solve for the unknown rate and state units

quiz.q: A 5 m ladder has its foot 4 m from the wall, moving away at 2 cm/s. At what rate (cm/s) is the height of the top changing?
quiz.explain: x dx/dt + y dy/dt = 0 with x = 4, y = 3, dx/dt = 2: dy/dt = −(4 × 2)/3 = −8/3. Negative because the top moves down.
quiz.mistake: Drops the negative sign or swaps x and y

quiz.q: C(x) = 2x² + 5x + 100 (₹). What is the marginal cost when x = 10?
quiz.explain: MC = dC/dx = 4x + 5 = 45 at x = 10.
quiz.mistake: Computes total cost C(10) instead of its derivative

quiz.q: R(x) = 3x² + 36x + 5 (₹). What is the marginal revenue when x = 5?
quiz.mistake: Evaluates R(5) instead of R′(5)

quiz.q: Sand pours at 12 cm³/s and forms a cone whose height is always one-sixth of its base radius. How fast does the height grow when h = 4 cm?
quiz.explain: r = 6h, so V = (1/3)π(36h²)h = 12πh³. dV/dt = 36πh² dh/dt ⇒ 12 = 36π(16) dh/dt ⇒ dh/dt = 1/(48π).
quiz.mistake: Uses r = h/6 instead of r = 6h

quiz.q: A balloon stays spherical. Its radius grows at 0.5 cm/s. How fast (cm³/s) is its volume growing when r = 2 cm, in terms of π?
quiz.explain: dV/dt = 4πr² dr/dt = 4π(4)(0.5) = 8π cm³/s.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to multiply by dr/dt

quiz.q: A man 2 m tall walks away from a 6 m lamp post at 5 km/h. Taking x as his distance from the post and s as his shadow length, which relation follows from similar triangles?
quiz.explain: Lamp height 6 over (x + s) equals man's height 2 over s: 6s = 2x + 2s ⇒ s = x/2. Then ds/dt = (1/2)(5) = 2.5 km/h.
quiz.mistake: Uses x instead of x + s for the big triangle's base

quiz.q: What does a marginal cost of ₹45 at x = 10 units mean?
options: The total cost of 10 units is ₹45
Producing the 11th unit costs about ₹45 more
quiz.explain: Marginal cost is the instantaneous rate of change of total cost, approximately the extra cost of one more unit.
quiz.mistake: Confuses marginal cost with total or average cost

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): When the foot of a sliding ladder moves away from the wall, dy/dt for the top is negative.
Reason (R): x dx/dt + y dy/dt = 0 with x, y, dx/dt > 0 forces dy/dt < 0.
options: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R explains A
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Since x dx/dt > 0 and y > 0, we need dy/dt < 0 to make the sum zero, which is why the top moves down.
quiz.mistake: Thinks both ends of the ladder move in the same direction

teach.ask: Gappu wonders: 'A ladder slides down a wall. How do I find how fast the top falls?'
teach.praise: Chirp-chirp! Link x and y, differentiate with respect to time, plug in values, and the minus sign shows the top going down!
teach.nudge: After you write the equation, what do you differentiate with respect to?

learn.hook: A Sensex chart rises and falls. Where it climbs, its slope is positive; where it dips, negative. The sign of f′ is the whole story.
points: f is increasing on I if x1 < x2 ⇒ f(x1) ≤ f(x2); strictly increasing if x1 < x2 ⇒ f(x1) < f(x2). Decreasing and strictly decreasing are defined similarly.
f is increasing at x₀ if it is increasing on some open interval around x₀.
If f′(x) > 0 on (a, b), f is strictly increasing on [a, b] (f continuous on [a, b]). If f′(x) < 0, strictly decreasing.
If f′(x) = 0 throughout, f is constant.
A constant function is both increasing and decreasing (not strictly).

example.q: Show that f(x) = x³ − 3x² + 4x is strictly increasing on R.
example.answer: f′(x) > 0 for all x, so f is strictly increasing on R.

learn.reallife: A home-loan EMI is an increasing function of the interest rate: for the same loan amount and tenure, a higher rate always means a higher EMI.

games.title: Strictly increasing or strictly decreasing on the interval?
items: 7x − 3 on R
e^(2x) on R
cos x on (0, π)
log x on (0, ∞)
−5x + 2 on R
sin x on (0, π/2)
x² on (−∞, 0)

games.title: Monotonic facts
items: If f′(x) > 0 on an interval, f is strictly increasing there.
This is the first derivative test for monotonicity.
x² is strictly increasing on R.
It decreases on (−∞, 0).
A constant function is increasing on R.
x1 < x2 gives f(x1) = f(x2), which satisfies ≤.
A strictly increasing function must have f′(x) > 0 everywhere.
x³ is strictly increasing but f′(0) = 0.
tan x is strictly increasing on (−π/2, π/2).
Its derivative sec²x is positive.

quiz.q: Which function is strictly decreasing on R?
quiz.explain: f′(x) = −3 < 0 for all x.
quiz.mistake: Picks a function that decreases only on part of R

quiz.q: On which interval is f(x) = sin x strictly decreasing?
quiz.explain: f′(x) = cos x < 0 on (π/2, π).
quiz.mistake: Picks an interval where cos x is positive

quiz.q: Why is f(x) = x³ strictly increasing on R even though f′(0) = 0?
options: Because f′(x) > 0 except at a single point, and x1 < x2 still gives x1³ < x2³
quiz.explain: f′(x) = 3x² ≥ 0 and vanishes only at x = 0; the definition x1 < x2 ⇒ x1³ < x2³ holds everywhere.
quiz.mistake: Thinks one zero of f′ breaks strict increase

quiz.q: Which statement about f(x) = log x is true?
quiz.mistake: Forgets that log x is defined only for x > 0

quiz.q: f(x) = cos x on (0, π) is
quiz.explain: f′(x) = −sin x < 0 on (0, π).
quiz.mistake: Forgets the minus sign in the derivative of cos x

quiz.q: Is f(x) = x² increasing at x = 0?
options: No; it is neither increasing nor decreasing at 0
quiz.explain: In every interval around 0, f decreases on the left and increases on the right, so it is neither.
quiz.mistake: Uses f(x) ≥ 0 as a reason for increase

quiz.q: For which value of k is f(x) = kx + 7 strictly increasing on R?
quiz.explain: f′(x) = k must be positive, so k = 2 works and the others do not.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the constant term 7 decides the direction

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): f(x) = e^(−x) is strictly decreasing on R.
Reason (R): f′(x) = −e^(−x) < 0 for all x.
options: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R explains A
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Since eᵗ > 0 always, the derivative −e^(−x) is always negative, which is why f strictly decreases.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the chain-rule minus sign

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How can I tell where a function goes up and where it goes down?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Positive derivative means climbing, negative means falling. The sign of f′ tells all!
teach.nudge: What sign does f′ have where the function is decreasing?

topics.title: Finding intervals of increase and decrease

learn.hook: Board paper favourite: 'Find the intervals in which f(x) = 2x³ − 3x² − 36x + 7 is increasing.' One factorisation, one sign chart, full marks.
points: Step 1: find f′(x) and solve f′(x) = 0 (also note where f′ is undefined). These points split the line into intervals.
Step 2: test the sign of f′ in each interval. Positive ⇒ increasing, negative ⇒ decreasing.
Write answers with intervals: strictly increasing on (−∞, −2) ∪ (3, ∞) style.
For trigonometric functions, work inside the given interval, e.g. [0, 2π].
To find a constant that makes f increasing on an interval, require f′(x) ≥ 0 throughout it.

example.q: Find the intervals in which f(x) = 2x³ − 3x² − 36x + 7 is strictly increasing or decreasing.
example.answer: Strictly increasing on (−∞, −2) and (3, ∞); strictly decreasing on (−2, 3).

learn.reallife: Transport planners model fuel cost against vehicle speed; finding where the cost function rises or falls shows which speed range is wasteful.

games.title: Sign-chart method
items: Differentiate to get f′(x)
Factorise and solve f′(x) = 0
Mark the roots on the number line
Test the sign of f′ in each interval
Write increasing and decreasing intervals

quiz.q: On which interval is f(x) = x² − 4x + 6 strictly increasing?
quiz.explain: f′(x) = 2x − 4 > 0 when x > 2.
quiz.mistake: Solves 2x − 4 < 0 by mistake

quiz.q: On which interval is f(x) = x³ − 3x strictly decreasing?
quiz.mistake: Reads the sign chart the wrong way round

quiz.q: For f(x) = −2x³ − 9x² − 12x + 1, on which interval is f strictly increasing?
quiz.explain: f′(x) = −6x² − 18x − 12 = −6(x + 1)(x + 2). This is positive between −2 and −1.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that the leading −6 flips the signs

quiz.q: Find the least value of a such that f(x) = x² + ax + 1 is strictly increasing on (1, 2).
quiz.explain: f′(x) = 2x + a > 0 on (1, 2) needs 2(1) + a ≥ 0, so a ≥ −2. The least value is −2.
steps: f′(x) = 2x + a is smallest at x = 1
quiz.mistake: Uses the right end x = 2 and gets −4

quiz.q: On [0, 2π], where is f(x) = sin x + cos x strictly increasing?
quiz.explain: f′(x) = cos x − sin x = 0 at π/4 and 5π/4. f′ > 0 on [0, π/4) and (5π/4, 2π].
quiz.mistake: Takes the interval where f′ < 0

quiz.q: Which statement about f(x) = x/2 + 2/x (x ≠ 0) is correct?
options: It is strictly decreasing on (−2, 0) and (0, 2)
quiz.mistake: Treats x = 0 as part of an interval

quiz.q: Show that f(x) = log(sin x) is strictly increasing on (0, π/2). Which is the key reason?
quiz.explain: f′(x) = cos x/sin x = cot x, which is positive in the first quadrant.
quiz.mistake: Uses a true fact that does not prove the derivative is positive

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): f(x) = x³ − 6x² + 12x − 18 is increasing on R.
Reason (R): f′(x) = 3(x − 2)² ≥ 0 for all real x.
options: Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
Both A and R are true and R explains A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: f′(x) = 3x² − 12x + 12 = 3(x − 2)², which is never negative, so f is increasing on R (in fact strictly).
quiz.mistake: Thinks f′ = 0 at x = 2 makes f decrease there

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How do I find exactly where a cubic function is increasing?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Solve f′(x) = 0, split the number line there, and check the sign of f′ in each piece!
teach.nudge: After finding where f′ = 0, how do you decide increasing or decreasing?

topics.title: Local maxima, minima and the first derivative test

learn.hook: A trekker on the Western Ghats reaches a peak: just before it the path climbs, just after it falls. That sign change is the first derivative test.
points: f has a local maximum at c if f(c) ≥ f(x) for all x near c; a local minimum if f(c) ≤ f(x) near c. The largest value over the whole domain is the (absolute) maximum value.
Critical points: c in the domain where f′(c) = 0 or f′(c) does not exist. Local extrema can occur only at critical points.
First derivative test: f′ changes + to − at c ⇒ local maximum; − to + ⇒ local minimum.
If f′ does not change sign at c (like x³ at 0), c is neither: it is a point of inflection.
Some extrema need no calculus: (2x − 1)² + 3 has minimum 3 since a square is ≥ 0; sin 2x + 5 lies between 4 and 6.

example.q: Find the local maxima and minima of f(x) = x³ − 6x² + 9x + 15.
steps: At x = 1, f′ changes from + to −: local maximum f(1) = 1 − 6 + 9 + 15 = 19.
At x = 3, f′ changes from − to +: local minimum f(3) = 27 − 54 + 27 + 15 = 15.
example.answer: Local max 19 at x = 1; local min 15 at x = 3.

learn.reallife: Farm scientists look for the fertiliser dose at which crop yield peaks: the slope of the yield curve changes from positive to negative there.

games.title: Classify the critical point
items: f′ changes from + to −
f′ changes from − to +
f′ is + on both sides
x = 0 for f(x) = |x|
x = 0 for f(x) = x³
x = 0 for f(x) = −x²

quiz.q: Which point is a critical point of f(x) = |x|?
options: x = 0, where f′ does not exist
quiz.explain: Critical points include points where f′ does not exist. |x| has a corner at 0, and that is its minimum.
quiz.mistake: Looks only for f′ = 0

quiz.q: For f(x) = x³ − 6x² + 9x + 15, what is the local maximum value?
quiz.explain: Critical points 1 and 3; f′ changes + to − at 1. f(1) = 1 − 6 + 9 + 15 = 19.
quiz.mistake: Gives the x-coordinate instead of the value

quiz.q: For f(x) = x³ − 6x² + 9x + 15, what is the local minimum value?
quiz.explain: At x = 3, f′ changes − to +, so f(3) = 27 − 54 + 27 + 15 = 15 is a local minimum.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the local maximum with the local minimum

quiz.q: What kind of point is x = 0 for f(x) = x³?
options: A point of inflection, neither max nor min
quiz.explain: f′(0) = 0 but f′ = 3x² ≥ 0 on both sides, so no sign change: neither maximum nor minimum.
quiz.mistake: Assumes f′(c) = 0 always gives an extremum

quiz.q: What is the minimum value of f(x) = 9x² + 12x + 2?
quiz.mistake: Reports x = −2/3 instead of the minimum value

quiz.q: Does f(x) = eˣ have a local maximum or minimum on R?
quiz.explain: f′(x) = eˣ is never zero and always exists, so there are no critical points and no local extrema.
quiz.mistake: Thinks f(0) = 1 is a minimum

quiz.q: For f(x) = x⁴ − 62x² + ax + 9 to have a local maximum at x = 1, what must a be?
quiz.explain: f′(1) = 4 − 124 + a = 0 ⇒ a = 120. (Then f″(1) = 12 − 124 < 0, confirming a maximum.)
quiz.mistake: Makes a sign slip with 124

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Every local maximum value of a function is greater than every local minimum value.
Reason (R): At a local maximum, f′ changes from positive to negative.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: 'Local' means only nearby comparison. A wavy function can have a local max lower than a local min elsewhere, so A is false. R is the correct sign-change rule.
quiz.mistake: Treats local extrema as absolute extrema

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How do I know if a critical point is a peak, a valley, or neither?'
teach.praise: Tweet! + to − is a peak, − to + is a valley, and no change is neither. The first derivative test rocks!
teach.nudge: What if f′ has the same sign on both sides?

topics.title: Second derivative test and absolute extrema

learn.hook: Sometimes checking signs on both sides is slow. The second derivative test decides max or min with one number.
points: Second derivative test: if f′(c) = 0 and f″(c) < 0, c is a local maximum; if f″(c) > 0, a local minimum.
If f′(c) = 0 and f″(c) = 0, the test fails; go back to the first derivative test.
Absolute extrema on a closed interval [a, b]: evaluate f at every critical point in (a, b) and at the end points a and b. The largest is the absolute max, the smallest is the absolute min.
A continuous function on a closed interval always has an absolute maximum and an absolute minimum.
Tangents and normals and approximations are not in the current CBSE syllabus.

example.q: Find the absolute maximum and minimum of f(x) = 2x³ − 15x² + 36x + 1 on [1, 5].
example.answer: Absolute max 56 at x = 5; absolute min 24 at x = 1.

learn.reallife: To find the highest and lowest temperature of a day between 6 am and 6 pm, you must check both the turning points of the temperature curve and the two end times, just like an absolute extremum on [a, b].

games.title: Absolute extrema on [a, b]
items: Find f′(x)
Find critical points inside (a, b)
Evaluate f at critical points
Evaluate f at a and b
Pick the largest and smallest values

games.title: Second derivative test
items: f′(c) = 0 and f″(c) > 0 means a local minimum.
The graph is concave up there.
f′(c) = 0 and f″(c) < 0 means a local minimum.
That gives a local maximum.
If f″(c) = 0, the point must be a point of inflection.
x⁴ has f″(0) = 0 but a minimum at 0.
End points must be checked when finding absolute extrema on [a, b].
The extreme value may occur at an end point.
A continuous function on a closed interval always attains an absolute maximum.
This is guaranteed for closed bounded intervals.

quiz.q: For f(x) = 2x³ − 15x² + 36x + 1 on [1, 5], what is the absolute maximum value?
quiz.explain: Values: f(1) = 24, f(2) = 29, f(3) = 28, f(5) = 56. The largest is at the end point 5.
quiz.mistake: Ignores the end points and reports the local maximum 29

quiz.q: Find the absolute minimum of f(x) = x² on [−2, 1].
quiz.explain: Critical point x = 0 gives 0; end points give 4 and 1. The smallest is 0.
quiz.mistake: Checks only the end points

quiz.q: Find the absolute maximum of f(x) = 4x − x²/2 on [−2, 9/2].
quiz.mistake: Picks the end-point value 63/8

quiz.q: For the same f(x) = 4x − x²/2 on [−2, 9/2], what is the absolute minimum?
quiz.explain: f(−2) = −8 − 2 = −10 is the smallest of −10, 8 and 63/8.
quiz.mistake: Drops the −x²/2 term at x = −2

quiz.q: Using the second derivative test, x = 1 for f(x) = x³ − 6x² + 9x + 15 is
quiz.explain: f″(x) = 6x − 12, so f″(1) = −6 < 0: local maximum.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up which sign means maximum

quiz.q: What does the second derivative test say about f(x) = x⁴ at x = 0?
options: x = 0 is a point of inflection
It fails because f″(0) = 0; the first derivative test shows a minimum
quiz.explain: f′(0) = 0 and f″(0) = 0, so the test is inconclusive. f′ = 4x³ changes − to +, giving a minimum.
quiz.mistake: Assumes f″ = 0 always means inflection

quiz.q: Find the maximum value of f(x) = sin x + cos x on [0, π].
quiz.explain: f′ = cos x − sin x = 0 at π/4, where f = √2. f(0) = 1, f(π) = −1. Max is √2.
quiz.mistake: Adds the maximum of sin and cos separately to get 2

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): The absolute maximum of f(x) = x on [0, 3] is at x = 3.
Reason (R): f has no critical points in (0, 3), so the extreme values occur at end points.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: f′ = 1 ≠ 0, so only end points matter: f(0) = 0, f(3) = 3. R explains A.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a function must have a critical point to have a maximum

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How do I find the very highest value of a function on a closed interval?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Check all critical points and both end points, then pick the biggest. Never forget the ends!
teach.nudge: Besides critical points, which other points must you check?

learn.hook: What size of square should you cut from the corners of a sheet to make the biggest open box? Calculus gives the exact answer, not a guess.
points: Method: name the variable, write the quantity to optimise as a function of ONE variable using the given condition, differentiate, find critical points, and confirm max/min with f″ or a sign check.
Two positive numbers with fixed sum S: product is largest when both are S/2.
Open box from a square sheet of side a, cutting squares of side x: V = x(a − 2x)², maximum at x = a/6.

Classic results: a rectangle of maximum area inscribed in a circle is a square; a closed cylinder of fixed volume has least surface when h = 2r; a cone of maximum volume in a sphere of radius R has height 4R/3.
Profit P = R − C is maximum where P′(x) = 0 and P″(x) < 0.

example.q: A square tin sheet of side 18 cm has equal squares cut from each corner and the sides folded up. Find the cut size for the largest box.
steps: Let the cut be x cm. V = x(18 − 2x)², 0 < x < 9.
example.answer: Cut 3 cm squares; maximum volume 432 cm³.

learn.reallife: Can makers want to hold a given volume using the least metal. Calculus says the best closed can has h = 2r, that is, its height equals its diameter.

games.title: Optimisation recipe
items: Choose a variable and draw a diagram
Write the quantity to optimise
Use the condition to reduce to one variable
Differentiate and solve for critical points
Confirm max or min and answer the question

games.title: Problem ↔ optimum
pairs: Two numbers with sum 24, max product
Rectangle of max area in a circle
Closed cylinder, fixed volume, least surface
Cone of max volume in sphere of radius R

quiz.q: Two positive numbers have sum 24. What is their maximum product?
quiz.explain: P = x(24 − x), P′ = 24 − 2x = 0 at x = 12. P = 12 × 12 = 144; P″ = −2 < 0 confirms a maximum.
quiz.mistake: Squares the sum instead

quiz.q: Two positive numbers have sum 16. What is the minimum possible sum of their cubes?
quiz.mistake: Gives just one cube, 8³

quiz.q: From an 18 cm square sheet, an open box is made by cutting equal squares from the corners. What is the maximum volume (cm³)?
quiz.explain: V = x(18 − 2x)² is maximum at x = 3, giving V = 3 × 144 = 432.
quiz.mistake: Uses the wrong cut size

quiz.q: Find the point on the curve x² = 2y nearest to (0, 5).
quiz.mistake: Minimises distance only along the y-axis and picks the vertex

quiz.q: A rectangle is inscribed in a circle of radius 5 cm. What is the maximum possible area (cm²)?
quiz.explain: The maximum rectangle is a square with diagonal 10, so side 5√2 and area 50 = 2r².
quiz.mistake: Takes the side as the radius

quiz.q: Profit P(x) = −x² + 40x − 100 (₹ thousand). For which output x is profit maximum?
quiz.explain: P′ = −2x + 40 = 0 ⇒ x = 20, and P″ = −2 < 0. (Maximum profit is 300 thousand.)
quiz.mistake: Reports the maximum profit instead of the output

quiz.q: For the same profit P(x) = −x² + 40x − 100 (₹ thousand), what is the maximum profit?
quiz.mistake: Forgets the −100 fixed cost

quiz.q: A closed cylindrical can must hold a fixed volume with the least metal. What is the relation between its height h and radius r?
quiz.explain: S = 2πr² + 2V/r. S′ = 4πr − 2V/r² = 0 ⇒ V = 2πr³, and V = πr²h gives h = 2r.
quiz.mistake: Assumes the height should equal the radius
